author: K. Y. Wise
title: Minnesota Legislature approves Fischer's water pollution alert bill with unanimous votes - North Ramsey News
text:
A bill introduced by Rep. Peter Fischer aims to bolster requirements for notifying the public and Tribal governments of water pollution discharges. The legislation seeks to improve communication following such incidents, according to the Minnesota State Legislature.
The measure secured passage in both chambers before being sent to the governor on May 6, 2026, after a 134-0 vote in the House and a 65-0 vote in the Senate.
Filed as HF4224 on March 12, 2026, during the 94th Legislature’s regular session, the formal description is: ‘Notice requirements for water discharges modified.’
An analysis below uses the actual bill text and provides interpretive clarifications of its main points.
The bill revises Minnesota Statutes 2024, section 115.061, expanding notifications for discharges that could cause water pollution. It requires individuals to notify the relevant agency promptly after a discharge, except when involving five gallons or less of petroleum. After agency notification, owners of public treatment works or sewer systems must alert potentially affected downstream public, including Tribal governments, using the best available communication means. Notices must specify time, date, and details of the discharge, health concerns, and contact points. The law also requires posting signs at impacted public areas, with further procedural guidance to come from the agency.
In the House, the tally included 66 Democrats and 68 Republicans in support.
The Senate vote featured 34 Democrats and 31 Republicans in favor.
Rep. Peter Fischer (Democrat-44th District) sponsored the bill, joined by co-sponsor Sen. Mary K. Kunesh (Democrat-39th District).
Fischer holds an AA from Lakewood Community College, awarded in 1979, and a BA from the University of St. Thomas, conferred in 1981.
Fischer became a Minnesota State House member in 2023, representing District 44A after succeeding Ginny Klevorn.
In Minnesota, bills are submitted in either the House or Senate and referred to committees for review. They advance to full chamber debate and voting if approved by committee. Identical versions must pass both chambers before the governor may sign, veto, or let a bill become law without signature. The state legislature meets yearly, typically starting in January, introducing thousands of measures each session though only some are enacted.
